summary: Eight Canadian historians become person entries (Tier 2): Gregory S. Kealey (workers' control and class analysis; political policing), Sylvia Van Kirk and Jennifer S. H. Brown (women and families in fur-trade society, 1980; compared as a pair), Sherry Olson (historical GIS: households on the cadastral lot; city building in Baltimore), Bruce Curtis (the educational state, inspection and the census), Allan Greer (peasant, lord and merchant; Colonial Leviathan; settler colonialism and beyond), Cole Harris (geographical dispossession in British Columbia) and Adele Perry (gender, race and a settler colony). Critiques include Kealey on region and on ethnicity apart from class, Curtis on the census as artefact, Greer on settler-colonial framing (2018–19) and on staples, Harris on cultural enrichment and on colonial-discourse studies, Perry on Van Kirk, and named Indigenous critics (LaRocque on Van Kirk, Napoleon on Harris). Roster rows, strand text corrections and strand additions follow from read texts.
authorization: User, 2026-10-14: 'propose a list of Canadian historians who need an entry'; 'tier 1 and 2 are obvious'; Sherry Olson: 'she is the key HGIS person in Canada'. Tier 2: data/extension-2026/canadian-person-candidates-2026-10-14.md.
rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13); a field-bound big idea counts. Each Tier 2 name carries a framework the Canadian historiography names: the new labour history's class analysis, fur-trade social history and its gender and family turn, historical GIS on the cadastral lot, state formation, colonial space and dispossession, gender and race in a settler colony. Each draft's NOTES.md records what was read in full, in part, through reviewers or not at all; most of the books were borrow-only and are cited through reviewers, labelled as such. The candidate list's description of Greer as a critic of liberal order was not supported by any text read and is not drawn. Conflict of interest: Olson's entry does not use chapter 2 of Bonnell and Fortin (2014), by the atlas owner, which does not mention her. Dissertation evidence is metadata only and never in entry text.

text_revisions.old: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Perry’s gender and race in colonial British Columbia (2001) are among the works most cited by this field’s PhDs but are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism.
text_revisions.new: Van Kirk’s women in fur-trade society (1980) and Perry’s gender and race in colonial British Columbia (1995, 2001) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism. They are compared here because each brought race into Canadian women’s history. McPherson (2000) credits Van Kirk’s research ‘and the critical debates it has aroused’ with ‘bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women’s history’. Perry (1995) traced the ‘scarcity model’ of white women’s experience in the West to colonial discourse, and faulted fur-trade historians, Van Kirk’s ‘brilliant account’ included, for explaining mixed-race relationships as the product of white women’s absence.
text_revisions.reason: Fixes 1.140, finding 1: the citation ranking is replaced with the comparison the read texts support (pe139_vankirk_mcpherson_2000, p. 82; pe139_perry_sick_1995, pp. 27–31 and p. 30 n. 8). Sources added through strand_list_additions.
